newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: GOLF-SINGH CLAIMS BIGGEST WIN AT RAIN-SHORTENED MEMORIAL.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-SINGH CLAIMS BIGGEST WIN AT RAIN-SHORTENED MEMORIAL.

text.p: It took three days to complete the third round of the rain-soaked Memorial Tournament, but when it finally ended on Monday Vijay Singh of Fiji had a victory he has dreamed about.
Singh won the tournament, which was reduced to 54 holes, by two strokes over Greg Norman and Jim Furyk.

He shot a five-under-par 67 for the third round at Muirfield Village to finish at 14-under-par 202. Furyk matched Singh's 67, while Norman fired an eight-under 64 -- most of it over the previous two days.
"This is the biggest win of my whole career," Singh gushed. "It's been my dream to win a tournament like this one, Jack Nicklaus' tournament.
"I'm really, really pleased to have finally won, I haven't won for two years," said Singh.
The Memorial was plagued by some four inches (10 cm) of weekend rain that saw the third round begin Saturday and end Monday with numerous interruptions along the way. The fourth round was cancelled.
Asked about the strain of playing a 48-hour round, Singh replied: "I wouldn't mind waiting to win here if it took 72 hours."

Scott Hoch, the second round leader who would have won had the round been completely washed out, injured his back on the 11th hole Monday and ended up shooting a 73. He finished tied for fourth at 11 under with with Tommy Tolles (71) and Lee Janzen (68).
Tournament host Jack Nicklaus had his best PGA Tour finish since a sixth place at Pebble Beach in 1995, ending up eighth after a 69 left him at seven under par.
"I'll have to hold back my retirement notice for a while. I'd have loved to have played 72 holes because I think I could have sustained what I was doing," Nicklaus said.
When play was interrupted Sunday afternoon, Singh was tied for the lead with Hoch at 12 under par and had just hit his drive on the par-five 11th hole.
"The break came at the perfect time," Singh said. "It was too wet yesterday to have reached the green from there.
"I thought a lot about the 3-wood shot, practiced it on the range this morning, and when I hit it it went like a dream."
The 231-yard 3-wood shot landed a foot and a half from the cup on the 11th green. Singh made the putt for eagle, which gave him the solo lead for the first time.
He went on to birdie the 15th hole, and when Hoch failed to get out of a bunker and double bogeyed 16, Singh had a three stroke lead.
"That took some of the pressure off me and I didn't concentrate the way I should have and missed the three footer for par on 17," Singh explained.
Safely on the 18th in regulation, Singh two-putted for par and the two stroke win -- the fourth title of his PGA Tour career and first since the 1995 Westchester Classic.
The win was worth $342,000 to Singh and brought him up to 17th place on the PGA Tour money list with a $495,956 total.
Singh said his victory had given him renewed confidence and raised expectations for the U.S. Open in two weeks.
"I think I'll be able to play a little bit more freely. A lot of pressure has been taken off me," he said.
Tiger Woods came crashing back to earth at the Memorial, shooting a 74 that left him tied for 67th place at five over par. Only John Daly, who shot 80, finished behind him.
Woods suffered the worst single hole score of his stellar professional career -- a quintuple bogey nine on the third hole -- which included two balls in the water and a three-putt.
The Masters champion will skip this week's Kemper Open, instead opting to prepare at home for the U.S. Open at Congressional.
